question: On a manual transmission vehicle, what should you do before taking your right foot off the brake to avoid rolling back when starting?
choice_b: Partly engage the clutch
choice_c: Shift into neutral
choice_d: Fully release the clutch immediately
explanation: The manual advises partly engaging the clutch before taking your right foot off the brake, and applying the parking brake if needed to keep from rolling back.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.1 Accelerating

question: If your drive wheels begin to spin because of poor traction while accelerating in rain or snow, what should you do?
choice_b: Shift to a higher gear immediately
choice_c: Take your foot off the accelerator
choice_d: Press the accelerator harder to power through
explanation: The manual states that if the drive wheels begin to spin, you should take your foot off the accelerator, since using too much power on poor traction can cause you to lose control.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.1 Accelerating

question: How should you hold the steering wheel while driving a commercial vehicle?
choice_a: With one hand while the other rests on the gearshift
choice_b: Loosely with one hand, to allow quick adjustments
choice_c: With both hands close together at the top of the wheel
choice_d: Firmly, with both hands on opposite sides of the wheel
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides so the wheel does not pull away from your hands if you hit a curb or pothole.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.2 Steering

question: When backing a commercial vehicle, why does the manual recommend backing and turning toward the driver's side whenever possible?
choice_b: Because the driver can see better and watch the rear by looking out the side window
choice_c: Because it uses less fuel
choice_d: Because it is required by federal law
explanation: Backing toward the right side is dangerous because the driver can't see as well; backing toward the driver's side lets the driver watch the rear of the vehicle through the side window.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: Before backing with the help of another person, what should the driver and helper agree on?
choice_b: The exact speed limit for the area
choice_c: A set of hand signals, including a signal for "stop"
choice_d: Which radio station to listen to
explanation: The manual advises working out a set of hand signals that both the driver and helper understand, and to agree on a signal for "stop," before backing begins.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: According to the manual, what do most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require to change gears?
choice_a: No use of the clutch at all
choice_b: Shifting only while stopped
choice_c: Single clutching only
choice_d: Double clutching
explanation: Most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require double clutching to change gears; vehicles with synchronized manual transmissions do not require it.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions

question: The manual identifies two special conditions where a driver should downshift. What are they?
choice_b: Before fueling and before an inspection
choice_c: Before starting down a hill and before entering a curve
choice_d: Before accelerating and before signaling
explanation: The manual lists downshifting before starting down a hill (to control speed without overusing the brakes) and before entering a curve (to help the vehicle stay stable) as the two special conditions.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions

question: According to the manual, how far ahead should most good drivers look while driving?
choice_b: 12 to 15 seconds
choice_c: 5 to 8 seconds
choice_d: 30 to 45 seconds
explanation: The manual states that most good drivers look at least 12 to 15 seconds ahead, which is about one block at lower speeds and about a quarter mile at highway speeds.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.4.1 Seeing Ahead

topic: Seeing to the Sides and Rear
question: When should you check your mirrors during a lane change, according to the manual?
choice_b: Only if another vehicle honks
choice_c: Before changing lanes, after signaling, right after starting the change, and after completing it
choice_d: Only after the lane change is complete
explanation: The manual lists four separate mirror checks for a lane change: before changing lanes, after signaling to check the blind spot, right after starting the change, and after completing it.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.4.2 Seeing to the Sides and Rear

question: What is a key characteristic of convex ("fisheye" or "bug-eye") mirrors found on many large vehicles?
choice_b: They show a wider area but make objects appear smaller and farther away than they really are
choice_c: They are only used at night
choice_d: They show a narrower area but make objects appear larger and closer
explanation: The manual explains that convex mirrors show a wider area than flat mirrors, but everything appears smaller and farther away than it really is, so drivers must allow for this distortion.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.4.2 Seeing to the Sides and Rear

question: When should mirror adjustment be checked, according to the manual?
choice_a: Only when a passenger requests it
choice_b: Once a year during annual inspection
choice_c: Prior to the start of any trip, and it can only be checked accurately when the trailer(s) are straight
choice_d: Only after an accident occurs
explanation: The manual states mirror adjustment should be checked prior to the start of any trip and can only be checked accurately when the trailer(s) are straight.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.4.2 Seeing to the Sides and Rear

question: What are the three rules for using turn signals given in the manual?
choice_a: Signal only in bad weather, signal loudly, and signal twice
choice_b: Signal early, signal continuously, and cancel your signal after turning
choice_c: Signal after you turn, signal briefly, and leave it on
choice_d: Signal only on highways, signal with lights only, never use hand signals
explanation: The manual gives three rules: signal early (before you turn), signal continuously (don't cancel until the turn is complete), and cancel your signal after you've turned.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.5.1 Signal Your Intentions

question: How does the manual say you should warn drivers behind you that you are about to slow down?
choice_b: Give a few light taps on the brake pedal to flash the brake lights
choice_c: Sound the horn continuously
choice_d: Turn on your headlights
explanation: The manual advises a few light taps on the brake pedal, enough to flash the brake lights, to warn following drivers that you will need to slow down.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.5.1 Signal Your Intentions

question: According to the manual, when should you use your horn?
choice_a: Only when directing traffic at an accident scene
choice_b: Continuously while passing any vehicle
choice_c: When needed to let others know you're there, since using it unnecessarily can startle others and be dangerous
choice_d: Never, since horns are not permitted on commercial vehicles
explanation: The manual states the horn can help avoid a crash and should be used when needed, but it can startle others and be dangerous when used unnecessarily.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.5.2 Communicating Your Presence

question: If you must stop on a two-lane road carrying traffic in both directions, where should you place your warning devices?
choice_a: 500 feet in front of the vehicle only
choice_b: Within 10 feet of the front or rear corners of the vehicle, and 100 feet behind and ahead of the vehicle
choice_c: Only 5 feet behind the vehicle
choice_d: Directly under the vehicle
explanation: The manual instructs placing warning devices within 10 feet of the front or rear corners to mark the vehicle's location, and 100 feet behind and ahead of the vehicle on a two-lane road.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.5.2 Communicating Your Presence

question: If you must stop on a road or shoulder, within how much time must you put out your emergency warning devices?
choice_b: 1 hour
choice_c: 10 minutes
choice_d: 1 minute
explanation: The manual states that if you must stop on a road or shoulder, you must put out your emergency warning devices within ten minutes.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.5.2 Communicating Your Presence

question: According to the manual, what three components add up to total stopping distance?
choice_a: Reaction distance, turning distance, and idle distance
choice_b: Perception distance, reaction distance, and braking distance
choice_c: Acceleration distance, cruising distance, and coasting distance
choice_d: Signal distance, mirror-check distance, and braking distance
explanation: The manual gives the formula: Perception Distance + Reaction Distance + Braking Distance = Total Stopping Distance.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.1 Stopping Distance

question: What is "perception distance" as defined in the manual?
choice_a: The distance traveled while the brakes are fully applied
choice_b: The distance traveled after the vehicle has come to a complete stop
choice_c: The distance traveled before you even see a hazard
choice_d: The distance traveled from the time your eyes see a hazard until your brain recognizes it
explanation: The manual defines perception distance as the distance the vehicle travels, in ideal conditions, from the time your eyes see a hazard until your brain recognizes it.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.1 Stopping Distance

question: The manual states the average driver's reaction time is what, and how far does the vehicle travel at 55 mph during that time?
choice_a: About 5 seconds, accounting for about 500 feet
choice_b: About 0.1 second, accounting for about 5 feet
choice_c: About 3 seconds, accounting for about 200 feet
choice_d: About 3/4 second to 1 second, accounting for about 61 feet
explanation: The manual states the average driver has a reaction time of 3/4 second to 1 second, which at 55 mph accounts for about 61 feet traveled before the brakes are physically applied.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.1 Stopping Distance

question: At 55 mph on dry pavement with good brakes, about how far does the manual say braking distance can be?
choice_b: About 419 feet
choice_c: About 1000 feet
choice_d: About 216 feet
explanation: The manual states that at 55 mph on dry pavement with good brakes, braking distance can take about 216 feet.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.1 Stopping Distance

question: At 55 mph, what is the minimum total stopping distance given in the manual?
choice_b: About 142 feet
choice_c: About 419 feet
choice_d: About 216 feet
explanation: The manual states that at 55 mph, a vehicle will travel a minimum of 419 feet total stopping distance when perception, reaction, and braking distance are combined.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.1 Stopping Distance

question: According to the manual, if you double your speed from 20 to 40 mph, how much greater is the impact and braking distance?
choice_b: 2 times greater
choice_c: 9 times greater
choice_d: 16 times greater
explanation: The manual explains that doubling speed from 20 to 40 mph makes the impact 4 times greater, and the braking distance is also 4 times longer.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.1 Stopping Distance

question: Why do empty trucks require greater stopping distances, according to the manual?
choice_b: An empty vehicle has less traction
choice_c: Empty trucks always travel faster
choice_d: Empty trucks have weaker brakes installed
explanation: The manual notes that brakes, tires, springs, and shock absorbers on heavy vehicles are designed to work best when fully loaded, and an empty vehicle has less traction, requiring greater stopping distances.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.1 Stopping Distance

question: About how much should you reduce your speed on a wet road, according to the manual?
choice_b: About one-tenth
choice_c: You should not change speed on wet roads
choice_d: About one-third (e.g., from 55 to about 35 mph)
explanation: The manual advises reducing speed by about one-third on a wet road, for example slowing from 55 to about 35 mph, since wet roads can double stopping distance.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.2 Matching Speed to the Road Surface

question: On packed snow, how much should you reduce your speed according to the manual?
choice_b: No reduction is necessary
choice_c: By a half, or more
choice_d: By one mile per hour
explanation: The manual states that on packed snow you should reduce speed by a half, or more, and on icy surfaces reduce to a crawl and stop driving as soon as safely possible.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.2 Matching Speed to the Road Surface

question: How does the manual describe "black ice"?
choice_a: Ice that is always visibly black in color
choice_b: Ice found only on bridges
choice_c: A thin layer of ice that is clear enough to see the road underneath, making the road look wet
choice_d: A type of road paint used near hazards
explanation: The manual defines black ice as a thin layer that is clear enough that you can see the road underneath, making the road look wet; watch for it when temperature is below freezing.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.2 Matching Speed to the Road Surface

question: According to the manual, hydroplaning can occur at speeds as low as what, if there is a lot of water on the road?
choice_b: 10 mph
choice_c: 70 mph
choice_d: 30 mph
explanation: The manual states that it does not take a lot of water to cause hydroplaning, and it can occur at speeds as low as 30 mph if there is a lot of water present.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.2 Matching Speed to the Road Surface

question: If your vehicle begins to hydroplane, what does the manual say you should NOT do?
choice_b: Release the accelerator
choice_c: Let the wheels turn freely
choice_d: Use the brakes to slow down
explanation: The manual instructs that if the vehicle is hydroplaning, you should not use the brakes to slow down; instead, release the accelerator and push in the clutch to let the wheels turn freely.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.2 Matching Speed to the Road Surface

question: What does the manual say you must use as the principal way of controlling speed on downgrades?
choice_a: The braking effect of the engine
choice_b: The trailer hand valve only
choice_c: Rapid, repeated hard braking
choice_d: The parking brake
explanation: The manual states you must use the braking effect of the engine as the principal way of controlling speed on downgrades, saving the brakes so you can slow or stop as needed.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.6 Speed on Downgrades

question: What does the manual identify as the number one cause of injury and death in roadway work zones?
choice_b: Vehicle breakdowns
choice_c: Speeding traffic
choice_d: Improper signage
explanation: The manual states that speeding traffic is the number one cause of injury and death in roadway work zones, so posted speed limits must be observed.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.6.7 Roadway Work Zones

question: What following-distance rule does the manual give for speeds below 40 mph?
choice_a: At least 5 seconds regardless of length
choice_b: At least one second for each 10 feet of vehicle length
choice_c: A fixed 2 seconds regardless of vehicle length
choice_d: One car length for every 10 mph
explanation: The manual's rule is at least one second for each 10 feet of vehicle length at speeds below 40 mph, with an additional second added at greater speeds.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.7.1 Space Ahead

question: If you notice you're being tailgated, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Increase your following distance and avoid quick changes in speed or direction
choice_b: Tap your brakes repeatedly to warn them off
choice_c: Speed up to get away from the tailgater
choice_d: Turn on your taillights as a signal
explanation: The manual recommends increasing following distance, avoiding quick changes, and not speeding up; it also specifically warns against tricks like flashing brake lights or taillights to discourage a tailgater.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.7.2 Space Behind

question: Why does the manual warn against assuming posted bridge and overpass heights are always correct?
choice_a: Posted heights only apply to buses
choice_b: Heights are only estimates and are never accurate
choice_c: Bridges are rebuilt every year
choice_d: Re-paving or packed snow may have reduced the clearance since the heights were posted
explanation: The manual cautions that re-paving or packed snow may have reduced clearances since heights were posted, and that an empty van is higher than a loaded one.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.7.4 Space Overhead

question: When making a right turn in a large vehicle that must swing into another lane, what does the manual advise about vehicle position?
choice_a: Keep the rear of the vehicle close to the curb to stop other drivers from passing on the right
choice_b: Turn wide to the left before starting the turn
choice_c: Straddle both lanes throughout the turn
choice_d: Stop completely before beginning any turn
explanation: The manual advises turning wide as you complete the turn while keeping the rear of the vehicle close to the curb, which stops other drivers from passing on the right.
source_note: Hawaii Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017, Hawaii: May 2023), State of Hawaii CDL Program / AAMVA, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.7.6 Space for Turns
